Editorial
For a long time, local knowledge has been ignored by the scientific 
community and sometimes even resisted. Now, it is regaining 
attention, and this shift is timely: the various consequences of global 
mechanization, along with crises related to climate change and health 
issues, are prompting us to re-examine those knowledge systems, 
practices, and expertise that have long been marginalized.
Local knowledge is rooted in detailed observations of ecosyste
ms and is passed down through generations orally, providing 
valuable keys to building a sustainable future. In recent years, this 
type of knowledge has been increasingly recognized. The United 
Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 
2007, affirmed the rights of indigenous peoples to own, control, and 
develop their traditional knowledge.
UNESCO has long played a pioneering role in this field. Through 
the "Local and Indigenous Knowledge Systems" (LINKS) program, the 
organization actively promotes exchanges between indigenous 
knowledge holders and scientists, particularly in the areas of 
ecological protection, water resource management, and natural 
disaster prevention. Biosphere reserves are a concrete example of t
his concept—bringing together researchers and local communities to 
jointly explore locally adapted solutions. This effort marks a si
gnificant shift: science is no longer seen as a singular, top-down form 
of knowledge, but as a bridge for dialogue between different 
knowledge systems. Additionally, the Convention for the 
Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage protects practices, 
techniques, and skills passed down through generations and 
recognizes their universal significance.
Local knowledge not only provides empirical data but also challenges the 
foundations of scientific paradigms from the perspectives of ethical values, the 
relationship between humans and nature, and long-term observational 
dimensions. In the fields of agriculture, traditional medicine, and climate 
science, such knowledge has long fostered numerous major innovations, 
whose sustainability often surpasses purely technology-driven solutions.
However, this recognition must be accompanied by safeguards—
ensuring the community's free and fully informed consent, achieving 
equitable benefit-sharing, and preventing exploitative plundering. 
Our goal is not merely to integrate local knowledge into the 
mainstream scientific system, but to promote cooperation that 
benefits all parties.
By promoting this type of knowledge, UNESCO reveals to us an 
unspoken truth: to understand and protect this world, we need to f
ully integrate the knowledge and traditions of all ethnic groups, 
which will bring us immeasurable benefits. True science, along with 
ethical standards that align with this diverse world, should provide an 
inclusive space for the expression of all forms of human civilization, 
allowing the vibrant flowers of human civilization to bloom freely.
Editor-in-Chief
Agnes Bardon

From indigenous peoples 
preventing wildfires through 
controlled burning, to Inuit weather 
prediction methods, and the 'zaï' zaï 
water harvesting technique used in 
some African countries, traditional 
indigenous practices around the 
world are rich, diverse, and effective, 
embodying the wisdom of indigenous 
peoples. In the context of ongoing 
climate change and biodiversity loss, 
this knowledge is particularly val
uable.

Wide Angle
4 |  UNESCO Courier · January-March 2026
Long before artificial satellites orbited the Earth, Polynesian 
navigators were already able to cross thousands of miles of open 
ocean by observing stars, swells, bioluminescence, and the flight 
paths of seabirds. In the Sahara Desert, the Tuareg have 
traditionally relied on celestial movements, sunlight, wind 
direction, and topographical features for navigation, although 
today their modern navigation methods rely more on landmarks 
and are mostly conducted during the day. Cognitive science 
research reveals that these navigation systems exhibit highly 
complex spatial reasoning abilities through diverse 
environmental cues, far surpassing the single-input methods 
used in laboratory studies in terms of integration.
There are countless examples of the value of traditional knowledge, covering multiple 
fields such as water resource management, agriculture and forestry, healthcare, and 
fisheries. These practices are far from being mere collections of techniques; they are 
expressions of a worldview. For instance, textile craftsmanship is another form of 
'navigation,' providing spiritual guidance. The woven skirts of the outer islands of 
Micronesia, and the striped weaving traditions of Ghana and Nigeria, transform 
community knowledge and cultural identity into symbolic pattern languages.
These practices represent comprehensive 
systems of knowledge. They encode, preserve, 
and pass on cognition from generation to 
generation. Today, indigenous communities 
around the world are defending their rights to 
protect such cultural heritage while actively 
articulating the value of traditional knowledge 
systems as parallel scientific frameworks.
As Fijian researcher Salanieta Kitolelei stated at the 2025 Second 
Pacific Islands Ocean Conference held in Honiara, Solomon 
Islands: "In essence, there is no difference—we are merely 
describing the same thing in different languages."
In recent years, traditional indigenous knowledge has gained 
recognition, particularly due to the promotion of international i
nstruments such as the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of 
Indigenous Peoples. However, cultural and commercial encroachments 
still pose a threat to it.
Guardians of Biodiversity
As the climate crisis intensifies and biodiversity sharply declines, 
the world is beginning to focus on knowledge systems that were 
once overlooked. According to United Nations data, indigenous 
peoples make up less than 5% of the global population, yet they 
safeguard about 80% of the world's remaining biodiversity. They 
are closely connected to their surrounding natural environment, 
nurturing valuable knowledge that deserves in-depth attention.
"We observe nature, observing plants and animals. We are the guardians 
of nature, possessing profound knowledge of our environment." Mbororo
Betty Bosi states, “Men are responsible for 
building most of the indigenous leaders, 
and Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, Chair of the 
23rd Session of the United Nations 
Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, 
pointed out in April 2024, 'This knowledge is 
not theoretical but the crystallization of 
wisdom tested through centuries of 
practice.'”
The skills and wisdom accumulated by indigenous peoples 
are not merely passed down through generations but are 
systematically compiled into complex knowledge systems. The 
textile techniques of the Pacific and Africa are powerful 
examples. Weavers in the Pacific region are well-versed in plant 
ecology, sailing dynamics, and cultural etiquette, while West 
African weavers excel in loom technology, natural dyes, and the 
language of symbolic patterns. In both regions, knowledge is 
transmitted through apprenticeships and cultural practices. The 
textiles themselves become "living archives" of knowledge, with 
their patterns, production processes, and the artisans' skills 
embodying the wisdom of indigenous peoples.
On Taumako Island in the Solomon Islands, women are the 
guardians of the land and sea. They harvest and process the 
pandanus tree (a small tree widely distributed in Polynesia, 
Micronesia, and other regions) to weave sails that power 
navigation—a skill that has been passed down for over three 
thousand years. As islander Delsie 
The skills and wisdom accumulated by 
indigenous peoples have been systematically 
compiled into complex knowledge systems.
Local and Indigenous Knowledge Systems Programme: 
Promoting Indigenous Knowledge
The UNESCO established the Local 
and Indigenous Knowledge Syste
ms Programme in 2002, aiming to 
mobilize the knowledge, skills, and 
practices of local communities and 
indigenous peoples to support their 
participation in environmental 
decision-making, particularly in the 
fields related to biodiversity and 
climate change.
The program aims to promote 
indigenous and local
knowledge holders, natural and 
social scientists, resource 
managers, and decision-makers to 
engage in dialogue, ensuring that 
local communities play an active 
and equitable role in governance; at 
the same time, it focuses on 
strengthening the transmission of 
elders' knowledge and seeking a 
balance between community local 
knowledge and global knowledge 
within the formal scientific system.
Currently, the LINKS 
Programme undertakes the f
unction of the technical support unit 
for indigenous and local knowledge 
within the Intergovernmental 
Science-Policy Platform on 
Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services 
(IPBES), providing support and 
expert advice to help the 
Biodiversity Platform more fully 
incorporate indigenous and local 
knowledge in its assessments.

Globally, the cultures, languages, and 
knowledge systems of indigenous peoples 
are extremely rich and diverse. These 
knowledge systems, developed over 
hundreds or even thousands of years, have 
made significant contributions to the crops 
consumed by humans today, traditional and 
modern medicines, as well as the fibers and 
materials used in home and clothing. 
Although often referred to as "traditional

ms are actually based on empirical 
observation and repeated practice, and like 
other knowledge systems, they c
ontinuously evolve with the assimilation of

environment.
Researchers and companies often seek 
indigenous knowledge of the characteristics 
of plants, animals, and other non-human 
elements within ecosystems to develop ne
w technologies and innovations. This 
process, sometimes referred to as 
'bioprospecting,' is common in fields such 
as agriculture and food, biotechnology, 
pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and forestry, 
leading to the development of various 
products sold globally.

potential users of indigenous knowledge must first 
obtain the explicit consent of the knowledge 
holders and sign agreements that detail the

In addition, the laws of an increasing 
number of countries require applicants 
for intellectual property (especially patent 
rights) to disclose the source of genetic 
resources or traditional knowledge used 
in their inventions. With the finalization of 
the 2024 World Intellectual Property 
Organization Treaty on Intellectual 
Property, Genetic Resources and 
Associated Traditional Knowledge, more 
countries may adopt such 'source 
disclosure' requirements.
However, despite the implementation 
of the aforementioned measures, biopiracy 
continues to occur due to exploitable 
loopholes in the system. For instance, one 
can circumvent regulations by acquiring 
genetic resources or traditional knowledge 
in countries where restrictive legislation has 
not yet been enacted, or by utilizing 
historical collections preserved before the 
convention's enforcement. Moreover, while 
the issue of patent abuse has received 
widespread attention, other forms of 
intellectual property, such as plant 
breeders' rights and trademarks, may also 
contribute to the improper appropriation of 
indigenous knowledge. Without significant 
reforms, these loopholes will persist, 
meaning biopiracy will remain an 
unfortunate reality.

However, since the mid-20th century, with 
new advancements in genetics, products 
based on biodiversity or derived from it 
have begun to be seen as "genetic 
resources." This coincides with innovations 
in the way the value of biodiversity is 
assessed—its value is no longer deter
mined solely by actual use but extends to 
potential applications.
In the 1990s, several new 
developments completely changed this 
situation. First, the World Trade 
Organization (WTO) agreements 
standardized intellectual property 
protection standards, altering the way 
countries protect intellectual property 
related to genetic resources. In 1992, the 
Convention on Biological Diversity 
brought genetic resources under national 
sovereignty, while also laying the 
foundation for a system to prevent the 
improper appropriation of traditional 
knowledge. Subsequently, the 2010 
Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit 
Sharing established an international 
model for negotiating asset use rules 
between users and providers of genetic 
resources and traditional knowledge.

Has Common Heritage Become 
Private Commodity?
The root of the biopiracy issue lies in a 
historic shift, where the international 
community no longer views biological 
resources as the common heritage of 
mankind, but rather as private assets.
The circulation of plants, animals, 
and other components of biodiversity 
globally, as well as the sharing of related 
knowledge among different groups, is 
not a new phenomenon. Even before the 
European colonial era, various species 
and the knowledge of their cultivation 
and use had already spread widely acr
oss the globe. For a long time, humans 
have traded domesticated animals, 
spices, medicinal herbs, food and 
beverages, and fiber products over great 
distances, often drawing on the 
knowledge created by other groups to 
learn how to use the acquired items.
